title: Lifting The Maximally-entangledness Assumption In Robust Self-testing For Synchronous Games
authors: Matthijs Vernooij And Yuming Zhao
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2222 (2026).

Robust self-testing in non-local games allows a classical referee to certify that two untrustworthy players are able to perform a specific quantum strategy up to high precision. Proving robust self-testing results becomes significantly easier when one restricts the allowed strategies to symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, which allow natural descriptions in terms of tracial von Neumann algebras. This has been exploited in the celebrated [MATH] paper and related articles to prove robust self-testing results for synchronous games when restricting to PME strategies. However, the PME assumptions are not physical, so these results need to be upgraded to make them physically relevant. In this work, we do just that: we prove that any perfect synchronous game which is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies, is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies. We then apply our result to the Quantum Low Degree Test to find an efficient [MATH]-qubit test.

.
tldr: The paper lifts the maximally-entangledness assumption in robust self-testing for synchronous games, proving that perfect synchronous games that are robust self-tests under symmetric projective maximally entangled strategies are also robust self-tests for all strategies.
motivation: Robust self-testing results in non-local games are often proven under the physically unjustified assumption of symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, so these results need to be upgraded to be physically relevant.
method: The authors use tracial von Neumann algebras and the framework of synchronous games to prove a general lifting theorem that removes the PME restriction, then apply it to the Quantum Low Degree Test.
result: They show that any perfect synchronous game that is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies, and obtain an efficient qubit test as an application.
conclusion: The work makes previous robust self-testing results for synchronous games physically meaningful and provides a new efficient qubit test via the Quantum Low Degree Test, advancing the theory of device-independent certification.

title: Escaping The Shadow Of Bell’s Theorem In Network Nonlocality
authors: Maria Ciudad Alañón, Emanuel-Cristian Boghiu, Paolo Abiuso, And Elie Wolfe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2213 (2026).

The possibility of nonclassicality in networks unrelated to Bell’s original eponymous theorem has recently attracted significant interest. Here, we identify a sufficient condition for being “outside the shadow of Bell’s theorem” and introduce a testable criterion capable of certifying the novelty of instances of network-nonclassicality which we call minimal network nonclassicality. We provide examples of minimally network nonclassical correlations realizable in quantum theory as well as examples coming from more exotic operational probabilistic theories. In particular, we apply these concepts to the simplest configuration of the 3-chain scenario (a.k.a. the bilocality scenario) to prove that certain correlations have escaped the shadow of Bell's theorem. While some of the examples herein are unprecedented, we also revisit more familiar examples of network nonclassicality in order to highlight the contrast between our approach versus prior approaches with respect to assessing novelty.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a sufficient condition and testable criterion to certify network nonclassicality that genuinely escapes the shadow of Bell's theorem, with examples in the bilocality scenario.
motivation: Network nonlocality often reduces to standard Bell nonlocality, so distinguishing genuinely novel network effects from Bell-type nonlocality is crucial for understanding nonclassical correlations.
method: The authors define a sufficient condition for being outside Bell's shadow and a criterion called minimal network nonclassicality, then apply it to the 3-chain/bilocality scenario and construct examples.
result: They provide quantum and exotic operational-probabilistic-theory examples of correlations that escape Bell's shadow, including a proof for certain correlations in the bilocality scenario.
conclusion: This framework offers a principled way to assess the novelty of network nonclassicality and contrasts with prior approaches, clarifying what is fundamentally new in network nonlocality.

title: Spatial Structure Of Multipartite Entanglement At Measurement Induced Phase Transitions
authors: James Allen And William Witczak-Krempa
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2211 (2026).

We study multiparty entanglement near measurement induced phase transitions (MIPTs), which arise in ensembles of local quantum circuits built with unitaries and measurements. In contrast to equilibrium quantum critical transitions, where entanglement is short-ranged, MIPTs possess long-range k-party genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) characterized by an infinite hierarchy of entanglement exponents for k[MATH]2. First, we represent the average spread of entanglement with "entanglement clusters", and use them to conjecture general exponent relations: 1) classical dominance, 2) monotonicity, 3) subadditivity. We then introduce measure-weighted graphs to construct such clusters in general circuits. Second, we obtain the exact entanglement exponents for a 1d MIPT in a measurement-only circuit that maps to percolation by exploiting non-unitary conformal field theory. The exponents, which we numerically verify, obey the inequalities. We also extend the construction to a 2d MIPT that maps to classical 3d percolation, and numerically find the first entanglement exponents. Our results provide a firm ground to understand the multiparty entanglement of MIPTs, and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

.
tldr: The paper uncovers long-range multiparty entanglement and an infinite hierarchy of entanglement exponents at measurement-induced phase transitions, with exact results via percolation mappings.
motivation: Measurement-induced phase transitions exhibit entanglement scaling distinct from equilibrium criticality, but the spatial structure of multiparty entanglement and its universal exponents remain poorly understood.
method: The authors introduce entanglement clusters and measure-weighted graphs to characterize average entanglement spread, then use non-unitary conformal field theory and percolation mappings to compute exact exponents in 1D and numerical exponents in 2D.
result: They conjecture exponent relations (classical dominance, monotonicity, subadditivity), obtain exact k-party genuine multiparty entanglement exponents for a 1D measurement-only circuit, verify them numerically, and find the first exponents for a 2D MIPT mapping to 3D classical percolation.
conclusion: The work provides a firm foundation for understanding multiparty entanglement in MIPTs and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

title: Universal Purification Dynamics In Real Non-unitary Quantum Processes
authors: Federico Gerbino, Donghoon Kim, Guido Giachetti, Andrea de Luca And Xhek Turkeshi
abstract: We study purification dynamics in monitored quantum processes governed by ensembles of quantum circuits in different random-matrix symmetry classes. We analyze the universal aspects that emerge away from the measurement-induced phase transition and inside the volume/weak measurement phase and in the scaling limit of large time and Hilbert space dimension. We present two toy models that reveal two complementary visions and provide quantitative access to universal scaling: (i) a discrete-time dynamic in which each time step corresponds to multiplication by a Gaussian random matrix; (ii) weak continuous-time monitoring that induces a Dyson Brownian motion of the eigenvalues of the density matrix. The first approach provides an algebraic characterization based on rotational invariance emerging in Kraus’s operator space, focusing in particular on the unitary and orthogonal cases, respectively and , with the Dyson random-matrix index. The second approach, on the other hand, allows for a unified treatment for any , thanks to the mapping of the Fokker–Planck evolution of eigenvalues onto the Calogero–Sutherland integrable Hamiltonian diagonalized in terms of Jack polynomials. We provide explicit expressions for the universal decrease of Rényi entropies. We show that, approaching the universal scaling limit, numerical simulations of different models agree with each other and with our theoretical predictions. Our results clarify the existence of different classes of universality for the purification process in hybrid quantum systems, accessible in random circuit architectures and weak measurement protocols.
tldr: The paper studies universal purification dynamics in monitored quantum circuits across random-matrix symmetry classes, deriving universal scaling of Rényi entropies via two toy models.
motivation: Understanding universal aspects of purification away from measurement-induced phase transitions and in the volume/weak measurement phase, with connections to random matrix theory and integrable systems.
method: Analyzes discrete-time Gaussian random matrix multiplication and continuous-time weak monitoring mapped to Dyson Brownian motion, using rotational invariance and the Calogero-Sutherland integrable Hamiltonian diagonalized by Jack polynomials.
result: Obtains explicit expressions for the universal decrease of Rényi entropies and shows numerical simulations agree with theoretical predictions across different models and symmetry classes.
conclusion: The results clarify distinct universality classes for purification in hybrid quantum systems, accessible in random circuit architectures and weak measurement protocols.

title: Non-stabilizerness And Violations Of Chsh Inequalities
authors: Stefano Cusumano, Lorenzo Campos Venuti, Simone Cepollaro, Immacolata de Simone, Gianluca Esposito, Daniele Iannotti, Barbara Jasser, Jovan Odavić, Michele Viscardi, And Alioscia Hamma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2214 (2026).

We study quantitatively the interplay between entanglement and non-stabilizer resources in violating the CHSH inequalities. We show that, while non-stabilizer resources are necessary, they must have a specific structure, namely they need to be both asymmetric and (surprisingly) [MATH]. We employ stabilizer entropy (SE) to quantify the non-stabilizer resources involved and the probability of violation given the resources. We show how spectral quantities related to the flatness of entanglement spectrum and its relationship with non-local SE affect the CHSH inequality. Finally, we utilize these results – together with tools from representation theory – to construct a systematic way of building ensembles of states with higher probability of violation.

.
tldr: The paper quantitatively studies how non-stabilizer resources and entanglement structure govern violations of CHSH inequalities using stabilizer entropy.
motivation: To understand what quantum resources beyond entanglement are necessary for Bell inequality violation, particularly the role of non-stabilizerness (magic).
method: The authors employ stabilizer entropy (SE) to quantify non-stabilizer resources, relate spectral flatness of the entanglement spectrum to non-local SE, and use representation theory to construct ensembles of states with higher violation probability.
result: Non-stabilizer resources are necessary for CHSH violation but must be asymmetric and satisfy a specific condition, and spectral properties of the entanglement spectrum affect the probability of violation.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic framework for building state ensembles with enhanced CHSH violation probability and clarifies the interplay between entanglement and magic in Bell nonlocality.

title: Fast Bosonic Control Via Multiphoton Qubit-Oscillator Interactions
authors: Noah Gorgichuk, Mohammad Ayyash, Matteo Mariantoni, And Sahel Ashhab
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2224 (2026).

We study the problem of [MATH]-fold rotationally symmetric bosonic state preparation, which is of great importance to bosonic quantum error correction, using a multiphoton interaction between an oscillator and an auxiliary qubit. We present an [MATH]-photon Law-Eberly ([MATH]LE) protocol that serves as an analytic baseline, alongside numerical optimal control calculations that further reduce state preparation time. We find that multiphoton control protocols substantially reduce preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords compared to schemes relying on standard linear interactions. Further, we achieve arbitrary control over the oscillator's Hilbert space by combining different multiphoton interaction orders. We also extend these control improvements to the preparation of rotationally symmetric multi-oscillator states. Lastly, numerical simulations using realistic planar superconducting circuit parameters validate the robustness of our scheme against qubit and oscillator decoherence. Our findings can significantly enhance the performance of bosonic codes on planar superconducting hardware, an important ingredient for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

.
tldr: The paper proposes multiphoton qubit-oscillator interactions to rapidly prepare bosonic code states for quantum error correction, validated with superconducting circuit simulations.
motivation: Bosonic quantum error correction requires fast and accurate preparation of nonclassical states such as binomial, cat, and GKP codewords, but standard linear interactions limit speed.
method: They derive an N-photon Law-Eberly analytic protocol and use numerical optimal control to design faster state preparation, combining different multiphoton interaction orders for arbitrary oscillator control and extending to multi-oscillator states.
result: Multiphoton protocols substantially reduce preparation times compared to linear schemes and remain robust against qubit and oscillator decoherence under realistic planar superconducting circuit parameters.
conclusion: These control improvements can enhance bosonic code performance on superconducting hardware, aiding scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Simulating Quantum Measurements Without Superposition Devices
authors: Gabriele Cobucci, Alexander Bernal, Roope Uola And Armin Tavakoli
abstract: Superposition is the core feature that sets quantum theory apart from classical physics. Here, we investigate whether sets of quantum measurements can be modelled by using devices limited to performing jointly diagonalisable measurements. This leads us to introduce classical measurement models, where many such devices are connected together through classical randomness and post-processing. Such classical measurement models are intermediate between the notion of commutative measurements and joint measurability. Towards understanding these models we (i) identify exact noise and loss rates at which all projective measurements admit a classical model, (ii) propose numerical methods to construct classical models for finite sets of measurements, and (iii) show how to construct witnesses for ruling out the existence of classical models. In addition, we show that classical measurement models also have operational implications in non-disturbance tasks where sequential quantum measurements are implemented with classical side-information. Our work provides a new approach to the role of superposition in quantum measurements.
tldr: The paper introduces classical measurement models to simulate quantum measurements using only jointly diagonalisable devices, establishing thresholds, numerical methods, and witnesses for the role of superposition.
motivation: Superposition is the key quantum feature distinguishing quantum from classical physics, but it is unclear which sets of quantum measurements can be simulated without superposition, motivating a resource-theoretic study of measurement incompatibility.
method: The authors define classical measurement models that combine jointly diagonalisable measurements via classical randomness and post-processing, then derive exact noise and loss thresholds, propose numerical construction methods, and build witnesses against such models.
result: They identify exact noise and loss rates at which all projective measurements admit a classical model, provide numerical methods for finite measurement sets, and construct witnesses that rule out classical models, with operational implications for non-disturbance tasks.
conclusion: Classical measurement models form an intermediate notion between commutative measurements and joint measurability, offering a new perspective on the role of superposition in quantum measurements.

title: Breaking The Orthogonality Barrier In Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2205 (2026).

Classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are a widely deployed and well-established technology, forming the backbone of modern communication and storage systems. It is well known that, in this classical setting, increasing the girth of the Tanner graph while maintaining regular degree distributions leads simultaneously to good belief-propagation (BP) decoding performance and large minimum distance. In the quantum setting, however, this principle does not directly apply because quantum LDPC codes must satisfy additional orthogonality constraints between their parity-check matrices. When one enforces both orthogonality and regularity in a straightforward manner, the girth is typically reduced and the minimum distance becomes structurally upper bounded. In this work, we overcome this limitation by using permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and by restricting the orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction, while preserving regular check-matrix structures. This design circumvents conventional structural distance limitations induced by parent-matrix orthogonality, and enables the construction of quantum LDPC codes with large girth while avoiding latent low-weight logical operators. As a concrete demonstration, we construct a girth-8, (3,12)-regular [MATH] quantum LDPC code and show that, under BP decoding combined with a low-complexity post-processing algorithm, it achieves a frame error rate as low as [MATH] on the depolarizing channel with error probability [MATH].

.
tldr: The paper constructs quantum LDPC codes with large girth by using permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and restricting orthogonality constraints to the active part of the construction, achieving low frame error rates under belief-propagation decoding.
motivation: Quantum LDPC codes must satisfy orthogonality constraints that typically reduce Tanner graph girth and structurally bound the minimum distance, preventing the classical girth-distance-performance trade-off from directly applying.
method: The author uses permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and restricts orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction while preserving regular check-matrix structures. This circumvents conventional distance limitations and enables a girth-8, (3,12)-regular quantum LDPC code.
result: The constructed code, under BP decoding combined with a low-complexity post-processing algorithm, achieves a frame error rate as low as [MATH] on the depolarizing channel with error probability [MATH].
conclusion: The work breaks the orthogonality barrier in quantum LDPC code design, enabling large-girth regular codes that avoid latent low-weight logical operators and exhibit strong decoding performance.

title: Multipath Wave–particle Duality With Exact Quantification Of Which-path Knowledge
authors: O Jiménez And L Neves L F Melo
abstract: A quantum system (quanton) traverses an interferometer with equally probable paths and interacts with another quantum system (detector) that stores path information in a set of symmetric states. In this interferometric framework, we present a systematic quantitative study of wave–particle duality based on entropic trade-off relations between quantum coherence, characterized by the relative entropy of coherence of the quanton state, and which-path knowledge, quantified by the mutual information obtained through detector-state discrimination. Unlike prior upper-bound-based formulations, we obtain an exact quantification of which-path knowledge for the discrimination strategies considered here, encompassing previously considered strategies and extending beyond them. A general optimal measurement achieving this is implemented through a state-separation map governed by a continuous parameter , followed by minimum-error (ME) discrimination of either the successful outputs only (standard approach) or both the successful and failure outputs (concatenated approach). Our framework identifies a strategy-dependent hierarchy that generally emerges in the tightness of the resulting duality relations. At , both approaches reduce to the ME measurement, which typically yields the tightest relation. For , each approach yields a distinct relation that generally becomes less tight as increases, with the concatenated strategy always yielding a relation at least as tight as its standard counterpart. We further characterize the saturation of these relations by identifying the sets of detector states that lead to it and show that nontrivial saturation occurs only for interferometers with a nonprime number of paths. From these saturating sets, we elucidate how the underlying structure of the quanton-detector correlations gives rise to this behavior and explains the lack of universal saturation in multipath duality relations for pure states.
tldr: The paper develops an exact entropic quantification of multipath wave–particle duality by relating quantum coherence to which-path knowledge through optimal detector-state discrimination strategies.
motivation: Wave–particle duality is a foundational quantum-information concept, but previous multipath duality relations often gave only upper bounds on which-path knowledge and left saturation conditions unclear.
method: The authors model a quanton in an equally probable multipath interferometer interacting with a detector that stores path information in symmetric states, and they derive trade-offs between the quanton’s relative entropy of coherence and the mutual information obtainable via minimum-error discrimination under standard and concatenated strategies.
result: They obtain exact duality relations, identify a strategy-dependent hierarchy of tightness, prove the concatenated strategy is always at least as tight as the standard one, and show that nontrivial saturation occurs only for interferometers with a nonprime number of paths.
conclusion: The work clarifies how quanton–detector correlations determine saturation behavior and explains the lack of universal saturation in multipath wave–particle duality for pure states.

title: Performance Of The Spin Qubit Shuttling Architecture For A Surface Code Implementation
authors: Berat Yenilen, Arnau Sala, Hendrik Bluhm, Markus Müller, And Manuel Rispler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2219 (2026).

Qubit shuttling promises to advance some quantum computing platforms to the qubit register sizes needed for effective quantum error correction (QEC), but also introduces additional errors whose impact must be evaluated. The established method to investigate the performance of QEC codes in a realistic scenario is to employ a standard noise model known as circuit-level noise, where all quantum operations are modeled as noisy. In the present work, we take this noise model and single out the effect of shuttling errors by introducing them as an additional so-called error location. This hardware abstraction is motivated by the SpinBus architecture and allows a systematic numerical investigation to map out the resulting two-dimensional parameter space. To this end, we take the Surface code and perform large scale simulations, most notably extracting the threshold across said two-dimensional parameter space. We study two scenarios for shuttling errors, depolarization on the one hand and dephasing on the other hand. For a purely dephasing shuttling error, we find a threshold of several percent, provided that all other operations have a high fidelity. The qubit overhead needed to reach a logical error rate of [MATH] (known as the "teraquop" regime [23] increases only moderately for shuttling error rates up to about 1 % per shuttling operation. The error rates at which practically useful, i.e. well below threshold error correction is predicted to be possible are comfortably higher than what is expected to be achievable for spin qubits. Our results thus show that it is reasonable to expect shuttling operations to fall below threshold already at surprisingly large error rates. With realistic efforts in the near term, this offers positive prospects for spin qubit based quantum processors as a viable avenue for scalable fault-tolerant error-corrected quantum computing.

.
tldr: A large-scale numerical study mapping the surface-code threshold across a two-dimensional parameter space that includes explicit spin-qubit shuttling errors, showing shuttling is tolerable below threshold up to surprisingly large error rates.
motivation: Qubit shuttling enables larger qubit registers for spin-qubit platforms but introduces extra errors whose impact on quantum error correction is unclear, motivating a systematic evaluation within a circuit-level noise model.
method: Building on the standard circuit-level noise model, the authors add shuttling as an additional error location (modeled as depolarization or dephasing) and perform large-scale surface-code simulations to extract thresholds and qubit overhead over the resulting two-dimensional parameter space.
result: For purely dephasing shuttling errors a threshold of several percent is found when other operations are high-fidelity, and the qubit overhead to reach the teraquop regime increases only moderately for shuttling error rates up to about 1% per operation.
conclusion: Practically useful error-correction regimes are predicted at shuttling error rates comfortably higher than those expected for spin qubits, supporting the viability of shuttling-based spin-qubit processors for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Generalising Aumann’s Agreement Theorem
authors: Matthew Leifer And Cristhiano Duarte
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2210 (2026).

According to Aumann's celebrated theorem, rational agents cannot agree to disagree. In other words, agents who once shared a common prior probability distribution and who have common knowledge about their posteriors cannot assign different probability distributions to a given proposition. Common knowledge imposes strong restrictions on assigned probabilities. In fact, Aumann's agreement theorem was one of the first attempts to formalise and explore the role played by common knowledge in decision theory. Recently, the debate over possible (quantum) extensions of Aumann's results has resurfaced. This paper contributes to this discussion. First, we argue that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory. Secondly, by building on the quantum argument, we show that agreeing to disagree is also forbidden in any generalised probability theory. The upshot is that in its probabilistic version, the agreement theorem is a direct consequence of how we choose to condition upon acquiring new information.

.
tldr: The paper proves that Aumann's agreement theorem extends to quantum theory and generalised probability theories, showing that rational agents cannot agree to disagree when they have common knowledge and a shared prior.
motivation: Aumann's agreement theorem is a foundational result in decision theory, and recent debate about possible quantum extensions motivates understanding whether common knowledge imposes similar constraints in quantum and generalised probabilistic settings.
method: The authors analyze agreement scenarios using quantum probability theory and generalise the argument to any generalised probability theory, focusing on the role of conditioning upon acquiring new information.
result: They show that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory and, more generally, in any generalised probability theory, deriving the agreement theorem from the principles of conditioning.
conclusion: The probabilistic version of the agreement theorem is a direct consequence of how agents condition on new information, extending its validity beyond classical probability.

title: Streaming Belief Propagation On Mixed-Alphabet Tanner Graphs For Practical Quantum Memory
authors: Kao-Yueh Kuo And Ching-Yi Lai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2207 (2026).

Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that can process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation. In practical quantum error correction (QEC), repeated syndrome measurements cause the number of potential error locations to grow rapidly with both code size and time. In this paper, we propose a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation (SM-BP) decoder. We construct a space-time Tanner graph across multiple rounds of syndrome extraction with mixed-alphabet error variables, preserving correlations arising from multi-qubit faults. Additionally, we propose an adaptive sliding window procedure that captures long error events across window boundaries and adjusts the decoding in real time. To enhance SM-BP, we introduce a technique of probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy effects and short cycles. Our simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for topological code families, including rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes. These results show that SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous QEC under circuit-level noise.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise, achieving high thresholds and strong error-floor performance for topological code families.
motivation: Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation, as repeated measurements rapidly increase potential error locations.
method: The authors construct a space-time Tanner graph across multiple syndrome extraction rounds using mixed-alphabet error variables, and propose an adaptive sliding window procedure plus probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy and short cycles.
result: Simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes.
conclusion: SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise.

title: Floquetifying Stabiliser Codes With Distance-preserving Rewrites
authors: Benjamin Rodatz, Boldizsár Poór, And Aleks Kissinger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2202 (2026).

Stabiliser codes with large weight measurements can be challenging to implement fault-tolerantly. To overcome this, we propose a Floquetification procedure which, given a stabiliser code, synthesises a novel Floquet code that only uses single- and two-qubit operations. Moreover, this procedure preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code. The new Floquet code requires additional physical qubits. This overhead is linear in the weight of the largest measurement of the original code. Our method is based on the ZX calculus, a graphical language for representing and rewriting quantum circuits. However, a problem arises with the use of ZX in the context of rewriting error-correcting codes: ZX rewrites generally do not preserve code distance. Tackling this issue, we define the notion of distance-preserving rewrite that enables the transformation of error-correcting codes without changing their distance. These distance-preserving rewrites are used to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into quantum circuits with single- and two-qubit operations. As we only use distance-preserving rewrites, we are guaranteed that a single error in the resulting circuit creates at most a single error on the data qubits. These decompositions enable us to generalise the Floquetification procedure of Townsend-Teague et al [83] to arbitrary stabiliser codes, provably preserving the distance and number of logicals of the original code.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a Floquetification procedure that converts arbitrary stabiliser codes into Floquet codes using only single- and two-qubit operations while provably preserving code distance and logical count.
motivation: High-weight stabiliser measurements are hard to implement fault-tolerantly, and existing Floquetification techniques only applied to specific codes such as the colour code.
method: Using the ZX calculus, the authors define distance-preserving rewrites that decompose arbitrary-weight stabiliser measurements into single- and two-qubit circuits, ensuring a single circuit error induces at most one data-qubit error.
result: The procedure generalises Floquetification to arbitrary stabiliser codes, preserves distance and number of logicals, and requires additional physical qubits whose overhead scales linearly with the largest measurement weight.
conclusion: Distance-preserving ZX rewrites provide a principled route to fault-tolerant Floquetification of general stabiliser codes, broadening the class of codes amenable to measurement-based Floquet architectures.

title: Heuristic And Optimal Synthesis Of Cnot And Clifford Circuits
authors: Mark Webster, Stergios Koutsioumpas, And Dan E Browne
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2212 (2026).

Efficiently implementing Clifford circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms. Linear reversible circuits, equivalent to circuits composed of CNOT\xspace gates, have important applications in classical computing. In this work we present methods for CNOT\xspace and general Clifford circuit synthesis which can be used to minimise either the entangling two-qubit gate count or the circuit depth. We present three families of algorithms - optimal synthesis which works on small circuits, A* synthesis for intermediate-size circuits and greedy synthesis for large circuits. We benchmark against existing methods, including rustiq, tket and qiskit and show that our approach results in circuits with lower two-qubit gate count. For encoding circuits, our methods outperform previous reinforcement learning results and find a lower two-qubit gate count circuit for the Golay code than previously known. The algorithms have been implemented in a GitHub repository for use by the classical and quantum computing community.

GitHub Repository

.
tldr: The paper presents optimal, A*, and greedy synthesis algorithms for CNOT and Clifford circuits that minimize two-qubit gate count or depth, outperforming existing tools and finding improved encoding circuits for the Golay code.
motivation: Efficient implementation of Clifford circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms, and linear reversible circuits composed of CNOT gates have applications in classical computing.
method: Three families of algorithms are developed: optimal synthesis for small circuits, A* synthesis for intermediate sizes, and greedy synthesis for large circuits, benchmarking against rustiq, tket, and qiskit.
result: The approach yields circuits with lower two-qubit gate counts than existing methods, outperforms previous reinforcement learning results for encoding circuits, and discovers a lower two-qubit gate count circuit for the Golay code.
conclusion: The algorithms are implemented in a public GitHub repository, providing a practical tool for the quantum and classical computing communities to improve circuit synthesis.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
authors: I.J. David, I. Sinayskiy, And F. Petruccione
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2204 (2026).

When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

.
tldr: The paper introduces randomised algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems on quantum computers, achieving better gate complexity than deterministic Trotter-Suzuki formulas.
motivation: Simulating open quantum system dynamics is crucial for many quantum applications, but existing methods like Trotter-Suzuki product formulas can be inefficient, especially for large systems.
method: They develop first- and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and a QDRIFT channel algorithm, deriving error bounds and step count limits without the mixing lemma.
result: Their algorithms maintain physicality and demonstrate gate complexity advantages over deterministic approaches, as shown by classical sampling implementations.
conclusion: Randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation can be extended to Markovian open quantum systems, enabling faster and more accurate simulations.

title: Exact Zero Modes In Interacting Majorana X- And Y-junctions
authors: Rik Mulder And Natalia Chepiga Bowy M la Rivière
abstract: We report the emergence of exact zero modes (EZMs) in junctions of two, three and four short interacting Majorana wires, equivalent to a chain with an impurity bond, Y- and X- junctions respectively. These EZMs arise from incommensurate short-range correlations and manifest as exact level crossings between in-gap states upon continuously tuning the interaction strength. In a junction of two chains the EZMs and parity switching appear as soon as the coupling across a junction is positive. This conclusion has a broad implication including the existence of EZM in quench- disordered systems. Remarkably, for junctions with multiple chains the in-gap states group up into sets of parity pairs–pairs of quasi-degenerate states with opposite parity attributed to the effective interaction of the outer edges of the junction. In the Y-junction with four in-gap states, we report EZMs not only within each parity pair but also between them. We demonstrate that this is attributed to an additional Majorana fermion localized at the center of the junction and protected by fermion parity symmetry. Therefore, coupling between the Majorana fermions at the outer edges of the junction is mediated by the central one. We argue that this is a generic feature of junctions with an odd number of arms. Surprisingly, in the X-junction we identify eight in-gap states arising from two Majorana degrees of freedom localized at the junction center. In contrast to the Y-junction, however, we show that the emergence of Majorana modes at the center of the X-junction is not topologically protected. As a result, the system parameters can be tuned such that the Majorana modes are expelled from the junction center and remain localized exclusively at the outer edges of the system.
tldr: The paper predicts exact zero modes and parity crossings in junctions of interacting Majorana wires, including X- and Y-junctions, and analyzes their protection and localization.
motivation: Majorana zero modes are central to topological quantum computing, but their behavior in interacting multi-wire junctions is not fully understood.
method: The authors study chains of short interacting Majorana wires with impurity bonds, corresponding to two-chain, Y-, and X-junctions, using analytical modeling and exact diagonalization of in-gap states.
result: They find exact level crossings as interaction is tuned; Y-junctions host a central Majorana mode protected by fermion parity, while X-junctions have two central Majorana degrees of freedom that are not topologically protected.
conclusion: The results reveal generic features of junctions with an odd number of arms and show that central Majorana modes in X-junctions can be expelled to the outer edges by tuning parameters.

title: Piston Control In A Two-ion Quantum Device
authors: E Ya Sherman And Andreas Ruschhaupt Jing Li
abstract: We propose a scheme for piston control in a two-ion quantum device with motion confined to orthogonal axes. In this system, one ion plays the role of a ‘classical’ piston driven by the Coulomb interaction with the other ion, whose quantum motion is controlled through modulation of its trapping potential. The stationary state is determined self-consistently, taking quantum effects into account. We identify a narrow quantum regime of the ground state connecting two broad classical regimes. We further design inverse-engineering protocols to control the motion of the ‘classical’ ion. The proposed control scheme provides a useful route toward controlled piston dynamics in microscopic quantum devices.
tldr: The paper proposes a scheme for piston control in a two-ion quantum device where one ion acts as a classical piston driven by Coulomb interaction with a quantum-controlled ion.
motivation: Controlled piston dynamics in microscopic quantum devices could enable new forms of quantum control and mechanical manipulation at the nanoscale.
method: Two ions with motion confined to orthogonal axes are considered; the stationary state is determined self-consistently including quantum effects, and inverse-engineering protocols are designed to control the classical ion's motion via modulation of the quantum ion's trapping potential.
result: A narrow quantum regime of the ground state connecting two broad classical regimes is identified, and inverse-engineering protocols are developed to control the classical ion's motion.
conclusion: The scheme offers a useful route toward controlled piston dynamics in microscopic quantum devices, potentially advancing trapped-ion-based quantum control.

title: Universal Dilation Of Linear Itô SDEs: Quantum Trajectories And Lindblad Simulation Of Second Moments
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu And Xiantao Li
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2223 (2026).

We present a universal framework for simulating [MATH]-dimensional linear Itô stochastic differential equations (SDEs) on quantum computers with additive or multiplicative noises. Building on a unitary dilation technique, we establish a rigorous mapping from the general linear SDEs [MATH] to stochastic Schrödinger equations (SSE) on a dilated Hilbert space. Crucially, this embedding is pathwise exact in that the classical solution is recovered as a projection of the dilated quantum state for each fixed noise realization. We demonstrate that the resulting SSEs are naturally implementable on digital quantum processors, where the stochastic Wiener increments are encoded directly by preparing the ancillary qubits. Exploiting this physical mapping, we develop two algorithmic strategies: (1) a trajectory-based approach that uses sequential weak measurements to realize efficient stochastic integrators, including a second-order scheme, and (2) an ensemble-based approach that maps moment evolution to a deterministic Lindblad quantum master equation, enabling simulation without Monte Carlo sampling. We provide error bounds based on a stochastic light-cone analysis and validate the framework with numerical experiments.

.
tldr: A universal quantum algorithm simulates linear Itô SDEs by unitarily dilating them into stochastic Schrödinger equations, with trajectory-based weak-measurement and ensemble Lindblad methods.
motivation: Simulating classical stochastic differential equations on quantum computers is challenging, and a rigorous mapping to quantum dynamics could enable efficient quantum algorithms for stochastic processes.
method: The authors use unitary dilation to embed a d-dimensional linear Itô SDE into a stochastic Schrödinger equation on a dilated Hilbert space, encoding Wiener increments in ancilla qubits, and develop two strategies: sequential weak measurements for trajectories and a deterministic Lindblad master equation for second moments.
result: The embedding is pathwise exact, the algorithms are implementable on digital quantum processors, error bounds follow from a stochastic light-cone analysis, and numerical experiments validate the framework.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical route to quantum simulation of linear SDEs without Monte Carlo sampling for moment evolution, with potential extensions to broader stochastic systems.

title: Reducing Spatial And Temporal Dimensionality In The Multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett Model
authors: Hongfei Zhan, Ernest W.Z. Pan, And Zhenning Cai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2201 (2026).

Focusing on the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, several techniques are adopted in this paper to reduce the spatial and temporal dimensionality, combined into an efficient algorithm. From a spatial perspective, an equivalent formulation of the Dyson series is presented. With the aid of a low-rank approximation, the spatial dimensionality of open quantum system simulations is halved. From a temporal perspective, the frozen Gaussian approximation is used to approximate both the evolution operator and the interaction operator in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model. This reduces the high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the truncation level of the Dyson series. Through these techniques, we design an efficient algorithm whose validity is verified through several numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double slit simulation.

.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient algorithm for simulating real-time dynamics of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model by reducing spatial and temporal dimensionality.
motivation: Real-time simulation of reduced density matrices in multidimensional open quantum systems is computationally challenging due to high spatial and temporal dimensionality.
method: It introduces an equivalent Dyson series formulation with low-rank approximation to halve spatial dimensionality, and uses frozen Gaussian approximation to reduce high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of Dyson truncation.
result: Numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double-slit simulation, verify the validity and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
conclusion: The algorithm enables efficient simulation of multidimensional open quantum systems, particularly the Caldeira-Leggett model.

title: Non-Gaussian Noise Magnetometry Using Local Spin Qubits
authors: Jonathan B. Curtis, Amir Yacoby, And Eugene Demler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2197 (2026).

Atomic scale qubits, as may be realized in nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, offer the opportunity to study magnetic field noise with nanometer scale spatial resolution. Using these spin qubits, one can learn a great deal about the magnetic-field noise correlations, and correspondingly the collective-mode spectra, in quantum materials and devices. However, to date these tools have been essentially restricted to studying Gaussian noise processes – equivalent to linear-response. In this work we will show how to extend these techniques beyond the Gaussian regime and show how to unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved way. We unveil two protocols for doing this; the first uses a single spin-qubit and different dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise. The second protocol uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to study spatially non-local cumulants in the magnetic noise. We then demonstrate the utility of these protocols by considering a model of a bath of non-interacting two-level systems, as well as a model involving spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising phase transition. In both cases, we highlight how this technique can be used to measure in a real many-body system how fluctuation dynamics converge towards the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size. We then conclude by discussing some promising applications and extensions of this method.

.
tldr: The paper proposes protocols using single and two NV spin qubits to measure higher-order non-Gaussian magnetic noise cumulants with nanoscale spatial resolution.
motivation: NV centers enable nanoscale magnetic noise spectroscopy, but existing techniques are restricted to Gaussian noise (linear response); extending to non-Gaussian noise can reveal higher-order correlations and collective-mode spectra in quantum materials.
method: They use dynamical decoupling sequences with one spin qubit to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise, and two-qubit coincidence measurements to probe spatially non-local cumulants, demonstrating with models of non-interacting two-level systems and correlated fluctuations near an Ising phase transition.
result: The protocols can unambiguously measure higher-order noise cumulants and show how fluctuation dynamics converge to the central limit theorem as bath size increases.
conclusion: The techniques offer a promising route to study non-Gaussian magnetic noise in many-body systems with local spin qubits.

title: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Simulation Of Stabilizer Circuits
authors: Muhammad Osama, Dimitrios Thanos, And Alfons Laarman
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2225 (2026).

We introduce new parallel algorithms for efficiently simulating stabilizer (Clifford) circuits on GPUs, with a focus on data-parallel tableau evolution and scalable handling of projective measurements. Our approach reformulates key bottlenecks in stabilizer simulation – such as Gaussian elimination and measurement updates – into GPU-tailored primitives that eliminate sequential dependencies and maximize memory coalescing. We implement these techniques in QuaSARQ, a GPU-accelerated stabilizer simulator designed for large qubit counts and many-shot sampling. Across a broad benchmark suite reaching 180,000 qubits and depth 1,000 (roughly 130M gates), QuaSARQ shows substantial runtime improvements, with up to 105[MATH] speedup, and over 80% energy reduction on demanding instances. Moreover, QuaSARQ consistently outperforms Stim, a state-of-the-art CPU-optimized stabilizer simulator, as well as Qiskit-Aer (CPU/GPU), Qibo, Cirq, and PennyLane. Finally, QuaSARQ exhibits a significant advantage in many-shot sampling on large workloads. These results demonstrate that our parallel algorithms can significantly advance the scalability of stabilizer-circuit simulation, particularly for workloads involving extensive measurements and sampling.

The open-source implementation of QuaSARQ is available at GitHub.

.
tldr: QuaSARQ is a GPU-accelerated stabilizer circuit simulator that parallelizes tableau evolution and measurement updates, achieving up to 105x speedup and over 80% energy reduction for large qubit counts.
motivation: Efficient classical simulation of stabilizer (Clifford) circuits is essential for benchmarking quantum error correction and large-scale Clifford workloads, but existing CPU simulators struggle with massive qubit counts and many-shot sampling.
method: The authors reformulate key bottlenecks in stabilizer simulation, such as Gaussian elimination and projective measurement updates, into GPU-tailored data-parallel primitives that eliminate sequential dependencies and maximize memory coalescing.
result: Across benchmarks up to 180,000 qubits and depth 1,000, QuaSARQ outperforms Stim, Qiskit-Aer (CPU/GPU), Qibo, Cirq, and PennyLane, with significant advantages in many-shot sampling and substantial energy savings.
conclusion: The parallel algorithms demonstrate that GPU acceleration can greatly advance the scalability of stabilizer-circuit simulation, particularly for workloads involving extensive measurements and sampling.

title: Unitary Causal Decompositions: A Characterisation Via Lattice Theory
authors: Tein van der Lugt And Robin Lorenz
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2218 (2026).

If a unitary transformation has a circuit representation with no directed path from input [MATH] to output [MATH], then [MATH] does not influence [MATH] through the overall unitary. Conversely, if a unitary satisfies a number of no-influence conditions, it is natural to wonder whether a circuit decomposition exists in which all of them are represented by absences of paths. Such decompositions are known as causal decompositions; determining their existence in general is a central open problem in the study of causal structure in quantum theory. We present progress towards a general solution by considering the special case of unitary causal decompositions, i.e. decompositions in terms of unitary circuits in the traditional quantum circuit formalism that do not require the generalisation to 'extended' or 'routed' quantum circuits prompted by earlier research on this topic. We identify a combinatorial condition that characterises precisely those sets of no-influence constraints [MATH] for which any unitary transformation satisfying [MATH] admits a unitary causal decomposition representing the constraints. Our approach is systematic, grounded in lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra, and offers hope for extensions to more general (e.g. routed unitary) causal decompositions in the future.

.
tldr: The paper characterizes which sets of no-influence constraints admit unitary causal decompositions using lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra.
motivation: Determining the existence of causal decompositions is a central open problem in the study of causal structure in quantum theory, and unitary circuits provide a standard formalism for testing such decompositions.
method: The authors identify a combinatorial condition, grounded in lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra, that precisely characterizes the sets of no-influence constraints for which any unitary satisfying them admits a unitary causal decomposition.
result: They obtain an exact characterization of the constraint sets that guarantee a unitary causal decomposition without requiring extended or routed quantum circuits.
conclusion: This offers progress toward a general solution for causal decompositions and suggests a path for extending the approach to more general routed unitary causal decompositions.

title: Sparse Quantum State Preparation With Improved Toffoli Cost
authors: Felix Rupprecht And Sabine Wölk
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2208 (2026).

The preparation of quantum states is one of the most fundamental tasks in quantum computing, and a key primitive in many quantum algorithms. Of particular interest to areas such as quantum simulation and linear-system solvers are sparse quantum states, which contain only a small number [MATH] of non-zero computational basis states compared to a generic state. In this work, we present an approach that prepares [MATH]-sparse states on [MATH] qubits, reducing the number of Toffoli gates required compared to prior art. We work in the established framework of first preparing a dense state on a [MATH]-qubit sub-register, and then mapping this state to the target state via an isometry, with the latter step dominating the cost of the full algorithm. The speed-up is achieved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry. The worst-case Toffoli cost of our isometry circuit, which may be viewed as a batched version of an approach by Malvetti et al., is essentially [MATH] for sufficiently large values of [MATH], yielding roughly a [MATH] improvement factor over the state-of-the-art. In numerical benchmarks on randomly chosen states, the cost is closer to [MATH]. With the improved isometry circuit, we examine the dense-state preparation step and present ways to optimize the joint cost of both steps, particularly in the case of target states with purely real coefficients, by outsourcing some sub-tasks from the dense-state preparation to the isometry.

.
tldr: Presents an improved algorithm for preparing sparse quantum states with reduced Toffoli gate cost compared to prior art.
motivation: Sparse state preparation is a fundamental primitive for quantum simulation and linear-system solvers, but existing methods incur high circuit costs dominated by the isometry step.
method: The approach first prepares a dense state on a sub-register and then maps it to the target sparse state via an efficient isometry circuit, which can be viewed as a batched version of Malvetti et al.'s method, with optimizations for real coefficients.
result: The worst-case Toffoli cost is essentially quadratic in the number of non-zero states for sufficiently large instances, giving roughly a square-root improvement over the state of the art, with numerical benchmarks showing even better performance.
conclusion: The improved isometry circuit reduces the overall cost of sparse state preparation and allows joint optimization of the dense-state preparation and isometry steps, particularly for real-valued target states.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut Via Qudit Swap Operators
authors: Igor Klep, Tea Štrekelj, And Jurij Volčič
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2203 (2026).

Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max [MATH]-Cut ([MATH]-QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with [MATH] vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on [MATH]. The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree [MATH]. This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the [MATH]-QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined [MATH]-QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For general [MATH], low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

.
tldr: The paper studies a qudit generalization of the Quantum Max Cut problem, analyzing the algebra generated by qudit swap operators and constructing a semidefinite programming hierarchy via noncommutative polynomial optimization.
motivation: Quantum Max Cut is a prominent 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and extending it from qubits to qudits may reveal new algebraic and computational structures relevant to quantum complexity theory.
method: The authors identify the algebra generated by swap operators as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and an additional relation, then use noncommutative polynomial optimization to build a converging semidefinite programming hierarchy; they also use representation theory and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients for exact solutions on complete bipartite graphs.
result: The hierarchy converges to the solution of the d-QMC problem, exact solutions are derived for a large class of complete bipartite graphs, and the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian is shown to distinguish isotypic components, with low-degree relations enabling efficient per-component optimization.
conclusion: The work provides an algebraic and algorithmic framework for higher-dimensional Quantum Max Cut, though its focus on complexity and Hamiltonian optimization lies outside the researcher's core interests.

title: Symmetry-enriched Topological Order In Tensor Networks: Defects, Gauging And Anyon Condensation
authors: Dominic J. Williamson, Nick Bultinck, And Frank Verstraete
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2199 (2026).

We study symmetry-enriched topological order in two-dimensional tensor network states by using graded matrix product operator algebras to represent symmetry-induced domain walls. A close connection to the theory of graded unitary fusion categories is established. Tensor network representations of the topological defect superselection sectors are constructed for all domain walls. The emergent symmetry-enriched topological order is extracted from these representations, including the symmetry action on the underlying anyons. Dual phase transitions, induced by gauging a global symmetry, and condensation of a bosonic subtheory, are analyzed and the relationship between topological orders on either side of the transition is derived. Several examples are worked through explicitly.

.
tldr: The paper develops a tensor-network framework for symmetry-enriched topological order, using graded matrix product operator algebras to represent domain walls and deriving anyon condensation and gauging-induced phase transitions.
motivation: To understand how symmetry-enriched topological order, topological defects, and anyon condensation can be captured in tensor network states and connected to the theory of graded unitary fusion categories.
method: Uses graded matrix product operator algebras to represent symmetry-induced domain walls, constructs tensor network representations of topological defect superselection sectors, and analyzes gauging and bosonic subtheory condensation.
result: Provides tensor network representations of defects for all domain walls, extracts the symmetry action on anyons, and derives the relationship between topological orders on either side of dual phase transitions.
conclusion: The work links tensor networks to graded unitary fusion categories and offers a systematic method for studying symmetry-enriched topological phases and their phase transitions.

title: A Brief History Of Quantum Vs Classical Computational Advantage
authors: Ryan Larose
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2198 (2026).

In this review article we summarize all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage to date. Our review highlights challenges, loopholes, and refutations appearing in subsequent work to provide a complete picture of the current statuses of these experiments. In addition, we also discuss theoretical computational advantage in example problems such as approximate optimization and recommendation systems. Finally, we review recent experiments in quantum error correction --- the biggest frontier to reach experimental quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm.

.
tldr: A review that surveys all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage, their subsequent challenges and refutations, theoretical advantage in optimization and recommendation problems, and recent quantum error correction progress toward Shor's algorithm.
motivation: To provide a complete picture of the current status of experimental quantum computational advantage claims and highlight remaining loopholes and challenges.
method: Literature review of experiments claiming quantum advantage, analysis of theoretical computational advantage examples, and a survey of recent quantum error correction experiments.
result: The review catalogues loopholes and refutations in prior advantage experiments, discusses theoretical advantages in approximate optimization and recommendation systems, and identifies quantum error correction as the biggest frontier for Shor's algorithm.
conclusion: Experimental quantum computational advantage remains contested with several claimed demonstrations later challenged, and scalable quantum error correction is essential for reaching advantage in Shor's algorithm.

title: Spin Seebeck Effect Under Periodic Heating: Three-temperature Approach
authors: A I Bezuglyj And L N Davydov
abstract: Within the framework of the phenomenological three-temperature approach, we considered the dynamics of the temperatures of electrons, phonons and magnons in a layered heterostructure consisting of a thin film of normal metal (NM), a layer of ferromagnetic insulator (FI) and a massive dielectric substrate. The dependence of the constant and variable components of the inverse spin Hall effect voltage on the thickness of the FI during periodic heating of the NM was obtained. From the agreement between the theoretical results obtained and experiments on Pt/YIG heterostructures, the values of a number of parameters characterizing the interaction of electrons and phonons with magnons were found.
tldr: The paper models the spin Seebeck effect in a normal metal/ferromagnetic insulator/dielectric heterostructure under periodic heating using a three-temperature approach for electrons, phonons, and magnons.
motivation: To understand the coupled thermal dynamics of electrons, phonons, and magnons in spin caloritronic systems and to extract microscopic interaction parameters from inverse spin Hall effect measurements.
method: A phenomenological three-temperature model describes energy exchange between electrons, phonons, and magnons via coupled differential equations.

title: Order Parameter Discovery For Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Nicola Mariella, Tara Murphy, Francesco Di Marcantonio, Khadijeh Najafi, Sofia Vallecorsa, Sergiy Zhuk, And Enrique Rico
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2217 (2026).

Quantum phase transitions reveal deep insights into the behavior of many-body quantum systems, but identifying these transitions without prior knowledge of order parameters remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce a method for constructing phase diagrams using the vector field of the reduced fidelity susceptibility (RFS), and demonstrate how information encoded in this vector field can be used to discover observables corresponding to order parameters. We apply our approach to well-established models: the Axial Next Nearest Neighbour Interaction (ANNNI) model, a cluster state model, and a chain of Rydberg atoms; and validate the discovered order parameters using eigendecomposition and finite-size scaling analysis, confirming the expected universality classes. Our results demonstrate that the RFS vector field offers a unified framework for phase characterization and order-parameter discovery that requires no prior knowledge of symmetry or transition type, while relying only on reduced density matrices of small subsystems.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a method that constructs phase diagrams from the vector field of the reduced fidelity susceptibility (RFS) to discover order parameters in quantum many-body systems without prior symmetry knowledge.
motivation: Identifying quantum phase transitions and their order parameters typically requires prior knowledge of the underlying symmetries or transition type, which is a bottleneck for exploring unfamiliar many-body models.
method: The authors build a vector field from the reduced fidelity susceptibility, which depends only on reduced density matrices of small subsystems, and use its eigendecomposition plus finite-size scaling to extract candidate order parameters.
result: Applying the approach to the ANNNI model, a cluster state model, and a Rydberg atom chain, the discovered order parameters reproduce the expected universality classes and phase diagrams.
conclusion: The RFS vector field provides a unified, symmetry-agnostic framework for phase characterization and order-parameter discovery in quantum many-body systems.

title: Evidence For Exceptional Points As Topological Defects
authors: Chia-Yi Ju And Szu-Ming Chen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2220 (2026).

Studies have shown that quantum states reside in a Hilbert space bundle. When a quantum system depends on continuous external parameters, these parameters define additional dimensions in the base space of the bundle. While much of the existing literature focuses on eigenstate subbundles, where geometric properties like Berry curvature arise, this work considers the entire Hilbert space bundle. Although the Hilbert space bundle has been found to be locally flat, suggesting that the system's topology may appear trivial, we revisit this assumption. Specifically, we examine how an arbitrary quantum state evolves when transported along closed parameter loops, a phenomenon characterized by holonomy. Our results demonstrate that nontrivial holonomy can emerge in the presence of exceptional points. Consequently, exceptional points naturally manifest as topological defects. Finally, we show that this nontrivial topology manifests in physical, time-dependent evolutions, providing a simple experimental signature to detect exceptional points by comparing state transport along distinct paths.

.
tldr: The paper argues that exceptional points act as topological defects in the Hilbert space bundle, leading to nontrivial holonomy that can be detected in time-dependent quantum evolutions.
motivation: Existing studies mostly focus on eigenstate subbundles and Berry curvature, while the full Hilbert space bundle is often treated as locally flat and topologically trivial. The authors revisit this assumption.
method: They analyze the holonomy of an arbitrary quantum state transported along closed loops in parameter space and examine how exceptional points affect this transport.
result: Nontrivial holonomy emerges in the presence of exceptional points, making them topological defects. This topology appears in physical time-dependent evolutions, allowing detection by comparing state transport along distinct paths.
conclusion: Exceptional points can be identified through a simple experimental signature based on path-dependent state transport, highlighting their topological nature.

title: Observation Of Even-denominator Fractional Quantum Hall States At Ν = 3/4 And 5/4 In The Lowest Landau Level
authors: Siddharth Kumar Singh, Chengyu Wang, Adbhut Gupta, Kirk W Baldwin, Loren N Pfeiffer And Mansour Shayegan
abstract: Two-dimensional electron systems (2DESs) confined to wide GaAs quantum wells (QWs) provide a unique platform to study exotic fractional quantum Hall states (FQHSs) because the 2DES has a bilayer charge distribution with significant interlayer tunneling. Precise control over the 2DES density allows the tuning of the interlayer tunneling over a wide range. Here, we present our discovery of new even-denominator FQHSs in the lowest Landau level (orbital index N = 0) at filling factors and 5/4 in an ultrahigh-quality 2DES confined to a 72.5 nm-wide GaAs QW. The ground states at and 5/4 both evolve from composite fermion (CF) Fermi seas to FQHSs as the density is raised so that interlayer tunneling is sufficiently reduced and the 2DES becomes two-component, signaled by the behavior of the FQHSs flanking and 5/4. The two-component nature of the and 5/4 FQHSs is also evident from their extreme sensitivity to the bilayer charge distribution symmetry: both states disappear quickly when the charge distribution is made asymmetric by only . We find a natural explanation for the 3/4 and 5/4 FQHSs in terms of two states linked by particle-hole symmetry, and using Scarola-Jain bilayer CF framework which is a generalization of the well-known, two-component, Halperin state ( state). Our observations elucidate the crucial role of competing energy and length scales in wide QW in stabilizing new ground states.
tldr: The paper experimentally discovers new even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states at filling factors 3/4 and 5/4 in the lowest Landau level of an ultrahigh-quality wide GaAs quantum well.
motivation: Wide GaAs quantum wells host bilayer 2D electron systems with tunable interlayer tunneling, offering a platform to explore exotic fractional quantum Hall states and competing energy/length scales.
method: Transport measurements on an ultrahigh-mobility 2DES confined to a 72.5 nm-wide GaAs quantum well, tuning density (and thus interlayer tunneling) and charge-distribution symmetry to probe the 3/4 and 5/4 states and their flanking states.
result: The 3/4 and 5/4 states evolve from composite-fermion Fermi seas to two-component FQHSs as density is raised, and both vanish rapidly when the bilayer charge distribution is made asymmetric, consistent with a particle-hole-symmetric Scarola-Jain bilayer CF description.
conclusion: The observations highlight the role of competing energy and length scales in wide quantum wells in stabilizing novel two-component even-denominator FQHSs.

title: Spinor Bose-Einstein Condensate As An Analog Simulator Of Molecular Bending Vibrations
authors: Ayaka Usui, Artur Niezgoda, And Manuel Gessner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2226 (2026).

We demonstrate that spinor Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) can be operated as an analog simulator of the two-dimensional vibron model. This algebraic model describes bending vibrations of molecules and, in the case of triatomic molecules, exhibits two phases where linear and bent configurations are stabilised. Spinor BECs can be engineered to simulate states that correspond to linear or bent triatomic molecules, with the Wigner function of the BEC encoding information about the molecular configuration. We show how quantum simulations of the bending dynamics of linear molecules can be realised, and how preparing a linear configuration in the bent phase leads to a dynamical instability. In the dynamics triggered by the corresponding instability, a significant amount of entanglement is generated, and we characterise the dynamics with the squeezing parameter and the quantum Fisher information (QFI). The scaling of the non-Gaussian sensitivity, described by the difference between squeezing and QFI, grows with the system size once the spinor system crosses from the linear to the bent phase, thus serving as a dynamical witness for the quantum phase transition.

.
tldr: Spinor Bose-Einstein condensates can simulate molecular bending vibrations, with entanglement and quantum Fisher information serving as dynamical witnesses for the linear-to-bent phase transition.
motivation: The paper aims to use spinor BECs as an analog quantum simulator for the two-dimensional vibron model, which describes bending vibrations in triatomic molecules and exhibits linear and bent configurations.
method: The authors engineer spinor BEC states to mimic linear and bent molecular configurations and characterize the resulting dynamics using the Wigner function, squeezing parameter, and quantum Fisher information.
result: Preparing a linear configuration in the bent phase leads to a dynamical instability that generates significant entanglement, and the scaling of non-Gaussian sensitivity (difference between squeezing and QFI) grows with system size across the phase transition.
conclusion: Spinor BECs provide a viable analog platform for simulating molecular bending dynamics and for witnessing quantum phase transitions via entanglement and metrological measures.

title: Time Symmetry In Quantum Theories And Beyond
authors: John H. Selby, Maria E. Stasinou, Stefano Gogioso, And Bob Coecke
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2221 (2026).

There exists a stark tension among different formulations of quantum theory as some are inherently time-symmetric while others are time-asymmetric. This tension is crisply captured when considering physical theories as theories of processes. We present the process theory of quantum physics, QPhys, which treats classical systems as internal to quantum theory. We provide three ways to incorporate time symmetry in QPhys. The first restricts the process theory of QPhys to one that satisfies an additional retrocausality constraint. The second is a novel approach, which extends the notions of causality and retrocausality to apply to systems along with processes. Utilizing this approach, we create a toy model for particle physics , where the causal and retrocausal systems correspond to particles and anti-particles respectively. The third approach extends QPhys to a supertheory that satisfies neither a causality nor a retrocausality constraint. To avoid unphysical predictions we modify either its composition rule or its processes.

.
tldr: The paper develops a process theory of quantum physics, QPhys, and explores three ways to incorporate time symmetry, including retrocausal constraints and a toy model for particles and antiparticles.
motivation: There is tension between time-symmetric and time-asymmetric formulations of quantum theory, which is sharpened when theories are viewed as theories of processes.
method: The authors present QPhys as a process theory and introduce three approaches: restricting QPhys with a retrocausality constraint, extending causality/retrocausality to systems and processes, and embedding QPhys in a supertheory with neither constraint.
result: They construct a toy model where causal and retrocausal systems correspond to particles and antiparticles, and they modify composition rules or processes in the supertheory to avoid unphysical predictions.
conclusion: The work offers a framework for reconciling time-symmetric formulations with quantum theory, though its primary contributions lie in quantum foundations rather than the user's listed research directions.

title: Truncation Uncertainties For Accurate Quantum Simulations Of Lattice Gauge Theories
authors: Anthony N. Ciavarella, Siddharth Hariprakash, Jad C. Halimeh, And Christian W. Bauer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2216 (2026).

The encoding of lattice gauge theories onto quantum computers requires a discretization of the gauge field's Hilbert space on each link, which presents errors with respect to the Kogut–Susskind limit. In the electric basis, Hilbert space fragmentation has recently been shown to limit the excitation of large electric fields. Here, we leverage this to develop a formalism for estimating the size of truncation errors in the electric basis. Generically, the truncation error falls off as a factorial of the field truncation. Examples of this formalism are applied to the Schwinger model and a pure U(1) lattice gauge theory. For reasonable choices of parameters, we improve on previous error estimates by a factor of [MATH].

.
