tldr: This paper develops a formalism to estimate truncation errors in the electric-basis encoding of lattice gauge theories on quantum computers, improving previous error estimates for the Schwinger model and pure U(1) gauge theory.
motivation: Quantum simulation of lattice gauge theories requires truncating the gauge-field Hilbert space, which introduces errors relative to the Kogut-Susskind limit; accurate error estimates are needed for reliable simulations.
method: The authors leverage Hilbert space fragmentation in the electric basis to analytically estimate truncation errors, showing factorial decay with field truncation, and apply the formalism to the Schwinger model and pure U(1) lattice gauge theory.
result: For reasonable parameter choices, the new error estimates improve upon previous ones by a factor of [MATH], and the truncation error is shown to scale factorially with the field truncation.
conclusion: The formalism provides a practical way to quantify truncation uncertainties for quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories, enabling more accurate resource estimates and simulation design.

title: Measuring A Quantum Measure Exceeding Unity
authors: Sanchari Chakraborti, Rafael D. Sorkin, And Urbasi Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2215 (2026).

The history based formalism known as Quantum Measure Theory (QMT) generalizes the concept of probability-measure so as to incorporate quantum interference. The resulting quantum measure [MATH] is defined for arbitrary events (sets of histories), not just for observables at a fixed moment of time. Thanks to interference effects, [MATH] can exceed unity, exhibiting its non-classical nature in a particularly striking manner. Here, in an optical experiment, we illustrate an ancilla based filtering scheme that gives operational meaning to the quantum measure. For a specific photonic event [MATH], we report a measured value of [MATH], which within errors agrees with the theoretical value of [MATH], while exceeding the maximum value permissible for a classical probability (namely [MATH]) by [MATH] upper or [MATH] lower percentile widths. The directly observed quantity is an ordinary detector probability [MATH] (or, with laser light, an equivalent power ratio); the value [MATH] is inferred via the calibrated relation [MATH] for our filter. If an unconventional theoretical concept is to play a role in meeting the foundational challenges of quantum theory, it seems important to bring it into contact with experiment as much as possible. Our experiment does this for the quantum measure.

.
tldr: An optical experiment measures a Quantum Measure Theory quantity that exceeds classical probability bounds, giving operational meaning to the quantum measure.
motivation: Quantum Measure Theory generalizes probability to incorporate quantum interference, allowing quantum measures to exceed unity, but experimental tests of this foundational concept are rare.
method: Using an ancilla-based filtering scheme with photonic events, the authors infer the quantum measure from ordinary detector probabilities via a calibrated relation.
result: They report a measured quantum measure value exceeding 1, agreeing with theory and exceeding the classical probability maximum by several percentile widths.
conclusion: The experiment provides operational meaning to the quantum measure, helping bring foundational Quantum Measure Theory concepts into contact with experiment.

title: Solving The Nonlinear Vlasov Equation On A Quantum Computer
authors: Tamás Vaszary, Animesh Datta, Tom Goffrey, And Brian Appelbe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2206 (2026).

The practical applicability of a recent Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with quadratic nonlinearities is investigated for the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators. The equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto the input of the quantum algorithm. Upper bounds for the query and gate complexities are derived in the limit of large grid sizes and found to be polynomially larger than the time complexity of the corresponding classical algorithms, primarily due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman-linearized evolution matrix. The convergence criteria are shown to impose severe restrictions on physically relevant plasma applications, requiring dissipation levels far exceeding those provided by the Krook operator.

.
tldr: The paper investigates the practical applicability of a Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook collisions, finding polynomial complexity overheads and severe convergence restrictions for plasma applications.
motivation: Quantum algorithms for nonlinear differential equations could offer advantages, but their practical viability for physically relevant plasma problems is unclear.
method: The Vlasov equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto a Carleman-linearized quantum ODE solver; query and gate complexity upper bounds are derived for large grids.
result: The quantum algorithm's complexity is polynomially larger than classical methods due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman matrix, and convergence criteria demand dissipation levels far beyond those from Krook operators.
conclusion: The approach faces significant obstacles for realistic plasma simulations, limiting its practical usefulness without substantial improvements.

title: Quantum Simulation Of Nuclear Dynamics In First Quantization
authors: Luca Spagnoli, Chiara Lissoni, And Alessandro Roggero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2200 (2026).

The study of real time dynamics of nuclear systems is of great importance to provide theoretical predictions of cross sections relevant for both terrestrial experiments as well as applications in astrophysics. First principles simulations of these dynamical processes is however hindered by an exponential cost in classical resources and the possibility of performing scalable simulations using quantum computers is currently an active field of research. In this work we provide the first complete characterization of the resource requirements for studying nuclear dynamics with the full Leading Order (LO) pionless EFT Hamiltonian in first quantization employing simulation strategies using both product formulas as well as Quantum Signal Processing. In particular, we show that time evolution of such an Hamiltonian can be performed with polynomial resources in the number of particles, and logarithmic resources in the number of single-particle basis states. This result provides an exponential improvement compared with previous work on the same Hamiltonian model in second quantization. We find that interesting simulations for low energy nuclear scattering could be achievable with tens of millions of T gates and few hundred logical qubits suggesting that the study of simple nuclear reactions could be amenable for early fault tolerant quantum platforms.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the resource requirements for simulating real-time nuclear dynamics on a quantum computer using first-quantized leading-order pionless effective field theory with product formulas and quantum signal processing.
motivation: Real-time nuclear dynamics are crucial for predicting cross sections in terrestrial experiments and astrophysics, but classical first-principles simulations are exponentially costly, motivating scalable quantum simulation.
method: The authors analyze the resource costs of time evolution under the LO pionless EFT Hamiltonian in first quantization using both product formulas and quantum signal processing.
result: They find polynomial scaling in particle number and simulation time, with resource estimates for realistic nuclear systems.

title: Charged Bose Polarons At Finite Momentum
authors: Grover Andrade-Sánchez And Arturo Camacho-Guardian
abstract: Charged impurities in quantum fluids have unveiled new classes of strongly correlated many-body states across condensed matter, ultracold gases, and hybrid atom–ion platforms. While previous studies have primarily focused on their ground-state and static properties, much less is known about their finite-momentum behavior, which governs transport, dissipation, and quasiparticle stability. Here, we investigate the momentum-dependent properties of a charged Bose polaron using a diagrammatic approach within second-order perturbation theory, explicitly accounting for the finite-range nature of the ion–atom interaction. We show that the interaction range introduces a characteristic momentum scale at which many-body dressing and dissipation are maximized, leading to a non-monotonic behavior of the damping rate and quasiparticle energy. In the high-momentum regime, we uncover a scaling law , signaling the suppression of many-body dressing and the recovery of quasi-free impurity dynamics, in stark contrast to the divergent behavior predicted by contact-interaction perturbative treatments.
tldr: The paper studies momentum-dependent properties of a charged Bose polaron using diagrammatic perturbation theory, revealing non-monotonic damping and a high-momentum scaling law due to finite-range ion-atom interactions.
motivation: Charged impurities in quantum fluids host strongly correlated many-body states, but their finite-momentum behavior—key to transport, dissipation, and quasiparticle stability—remains largely unexplored.
method: The authors use a diagrammatic approach within second-order perturbation theory, explicitly including the finite-range nature of the ion-atom interaction to compute momentum-dependent quasiparticle properties.
result: They find a characteristic momentum scale that maximizes many-body dressing and dissipation, leading to non-monotonic damping rate and quasiparticle energy, and uncover a high-momentum scaling law that contrasts with contact-interaction predictions.
conclusion: Finite-range interactions qualitatively alter the finite-momentum physics of charged Bose polarons, suppressing many-body dressing at high momentum and restoring quasi-free impurity dynamics.

title: Single Photon Zeptosecond Interferometry
authors: Geoffrey R Harrison, Tobias Saule, R Esteban Goetz, George N Gibson, Camilo Granados, Bikash K Das, Marcelo F Ciappina, Anh-Thu Le And Carlos A Trallero-Herrero
abstract: We demonstrate the generation of a train of attosecond XUV pulses that are in a superposition of wavefront states. Such superposition yields a high precision, self-referencing, common path XUV interferometer setup to produce pairs of spatially separated and independently controllable XUV pulses that are locked in phase and time with a temporal jitter of 3.5 zs (zs = zeptoseconds = s ). In our approach, we can independently control the relative phase/delay of the two optical beams with a resolution of 52 zs. Since the jitter is on the order of the Compton time scale , we explore the level of correlation between the non-local photons by comparing different spatial mode superpositions. Further, thanks to the stability of the interferometer we can retrieve the interference pattern through photon counting. Through post-selection of different particle events we can analyze one, two or more photon events. We argue that this zeptosecond level of temporal precision will open the door for new dynamical quantum electrodynamics (QED) tests at lower intensities while photon counting experiments can also have an impact on the emerging field of quantum light in strong fields. We also discuss the potential impact on other areas, such as time-dependent QED, imaging, measurements of non-locality, and molecular quantum tomography.
tldr: The paper demonstrates an attosecond XUV interferometer that generates phase-locked pulse pairs with zeptosecond jitter for probing QED and non-local photon correlations.
motivation: To achieve extreme temporal precision for dynamical quantum electrodynamics tests and to explore non-local photon correlations at lower intensities.
method: They generate a train of attosecond XUV pulses in a superposition of wavefront states, forming a self-referencing common-path interferometer with independent spatial and temporal control.
result: They achieve 3.5 zeptosecond temporal jitter and 52 zeptosecond phase/delay resolution, retrieving interference patterns via photon counting and post-selection of multi-photon events.
conclusion: This zeptosecond-level precision may enable new QED tests and impact quantum light in strong fields, imaging, measurements of non-locality, and molecular quantum tomography.

title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy With A Resonant Dichromatic Field: Role Of Geometric Phase
authors: Axel Stenquist And Jan Marcus Dahlström Evan Munaro-Langloÿs
abstract: We investigate geometric-phase control in resonantly driven two-level atoms exposed to near-degenerate dichromatic laser pulses. In contrast to conventional two-colour schemes based on widely separated frequencies, the closely spaced frequency components generate a slowly varying beating envelope that repeatedly reverses the pseudo-spin rotation on the Bloch sphere. This enables coherent control of the geometric phase accumulated during Rabi dynamics and strongly modifies the resulting photoelectron spectra. Using an exactly solvable model for flat-top pulse envelopes, we derive the essential-state dynamics analytically and analyse photoionization induced both by an auxiliary field and by the dichromatic driving field itself. We show that the formation of Autler–Townes (AT) doublets can be interpreted in terms of destructive interference associated with geometric phases acquired during completed pseudo-spin rotations. Beyond the canonical AT regime, beat-induced reversal dynamics lead to qualitatively different spectral structures, including re-emergent central peaks and higher-order sidebands. These effects originate from the nonuniform temporal evolution induced by the beating envelope, which modifies the balance between positive and negative excitation amplitudes. Our results establish beating-field control as a route toward engineering geometric-phase interference in ultrafast light–matter interactions and suggest broader applications in coherent control of atoms, molecules, and x-ray-driven systems.
tldr: The paper studies geometric-phase control in resonantly driven two-level atoms exposed to near-degenerate dichromatic laser pulses and its effect on photoelectron spectra.
motivation: Conventional two-colour schemes use widely separated frequencies, but closely spaced frequency components can generate a slowly varying beating envelope that repeatedly reverses pseudo-spin rotation on the Bloch sphere.
method: Using an exactly solvable model for flat-top pulse envelopes, the authors derive the essential-state dynamics analytically and analyse photoionization induced by an auxiliary field and by the dichromatic driving field itself.
result: They show that Autler–Townes doublets can be interpreted via destructive interference from geometric phases acquired during completed pseudo-spin rotations, and that beat-induced reversal dynamics lead to re-emergent central peaks and higher-order sidebands.
conclusion: Beating-field control provides a route toward engineering geometric-phase interference in ultrafast light–matter interactions, with potential applications in coherent control of atoms, molecules, and x-ray-driven systems.

title: Magnetic-field-induced Nondipole Effect In Strong Field Frustrated Double Ionization
authors: Linna Zhang, Mingzheng Wei, Luling Jin, Huipeng Kang And Xiaojun Liu
abstract: Strong field atomic frustrated double ionization (FDI) represents a novel approach for ultrafast preparation and control of highly excited ions. A comprehensive understanding of its mechanism is of fundamental significance. However, current interpretations are restricted to the dipole approximation. Here, the nondipole effect in FDI of Ar is investigated using a classical ensemble model, in which the magnetic component of the laser field is fully accounted for. We show that the magnetic field induces positive momentum of photoelectrons along the laser propagation direction, which depends on the laser intensity. By tracing the electron trajectories, it is found that the linear momentum transfer to photoelectrons is considerably enhanced by recollision. The ionization time distribution of electrons and corresponding momenta play important roles in the momentum transfer. The subcycle evolution of magnetic fields is related to the variation of momentum transfer for positive and negative momentum of photoelectrons along the laser polarization. This work provides an intuitive insight into the nondipole effect in FDI and offers a scheme for probing ultrafast magnetic fields and manipulating the linear momentum transfer.
tldr: This paper investigates the magnetic-field-induced nondipole effect in strong-field frustrated double ionization of argon using a classical ensemble model.
motivation: Frustrated double ionization offers a route to prepare and control highly excited ions, but existing interpretations rely on the dipole approximation and neglect magnetic-field effects.
method: The authors employ a classical ensemble model that fully accounts for the magnetic component of the laser field to simulate nondipole dynamics in strong-field frustrated double ionization of Ar.
result: The magnetic field imparts positive momentum to photoelectrons along the laser propagation direction, with recollision enhancing linear momentum transfer and subcycle magnetic field evolution shaping the momentum distribution.
conclusion: The work provides an intuitive understanding of nondipole effects in frustrated double ionization and suggests a scheme for probing ultrafast magnetic fields and manipulating linear momentum transfer.

title: Electrical Manipulation Of Centrosymmetric Antiferromagnets By Néel Torque
authors: Jin Cao, Weikang Wu, Huiying Liu, Shen Lai, Cong Xiao, Qian Niu, X C Xie And Shengyuan A Yang
abstract: Electric control of Néel vector is a central task of antiferromagnetic (AFM) spintronics. The major scheme so far has relied on the Néel spin–orbit torque, which however is restricted to AFMs with broken inversion symmetry. Here, we explore a nonlinear Néel torque, uniquely enabling electric control in the vast class of centrosymmetric AFMs including altermagnets, where the existing scheme fails. This new type of Néel torque operates in both AFM metals and insulators, and can appear in all collinear AFM configurations in all the 122 magnetic point groups. Combined with first-principles calculations, we predict significant effects in centrosymmetric AFMs MnRh, MnBi Te and altermagnet CrSb. Our work offers a new and general strategy for Néel torque, significantly broadens the scope of electric control of AFM systems, and opens a new arena in the field of AFM spintronics.
tldr: The paper proposes a nonlinear 'Néel torque' mechanism that enables electrical control of the Néel vector in centrosymmetric antiferromagnets and altermagnets, where conventional Néel spin–orbit torque fails.
motivation: Electric control of the Néel vector is a central goal of antiferromagnetic spintronics, but the established Néel spin–orbit torque mechanism only works in antiferromagnets with broken inversion symmetry, excluding the vast class of centrosymmetric materials.
method: The authors derive a nonlinear Néel torque mechanism using symmetry analysis across all 122 magnetic point groups, and verify significant effects via first-principles calculations for MnRh, MnBi2Te4, and the altermagnet CrSb.
result: The predicted torque operates in both AFM metals and insulators and appears in all collinear AFM configurations, yielding significant effects in centrosymmetric antiferromagnets and altermagnets.
conclusion: The work provides a general strategy for Néel torque, broadening the scope of electric control in antiferromagnetic systems and opening a new direction in AFM spintronics.

title: Pressure-induced Ising Superconductivity In Organic-intercalated 1T-TaS2
authors: Jiaqi Chen, Shuyang Wang, Lixuan Yu, Xuliang Chen, Chao An, Yonghui Zhou, Yilin Wang And Zhaorong Yang
abstract: Layered transition metal dichalcogenides host a rich landscape of correlated electronic phases that are profoundly sensitive to interlayer coupling. Although both thinning and pressure have been individually used to tune these properties, the high-pressure behavior of low-dimensional systems remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a synergistic tuning strategy by combination of organic cation intercalation and pressure to simulate the properties of low-dimensional materials under pressure. We show that intercalating cetyltrimethylammonium cations into the bulk 1T-TaS2 significantly weakens the interlayer coupling and leads to an effective reduction in dimensionality. Moreover, the intercalated sample exhibits distinct features under high pressure as compared with non-intercalated one. The superconductivity in the intercalated sample is induced accompanied by a complete suppression of nearly commensurate charge density wave order, differing from the melting of commensurate state in the non-intercalated case. Upon further compression up to 58.1 GPa, the superconductivity displays a dome-shaped evolution, also without showing re-enhancement that presented in the non-intercalated sample. More strikingly, the superconductivity in the intercalated 1T-TaS2 displays signatures of Ising superconductivity, with its in-plane upper critical field exceeding twice the Pauli paramagnetic limit. Our findings not only provide a powerful route for tuning the collective electronic states but also open up possibilities in searching for emergent phenomena in low-dimensional materials.
tldr: Organic cation intercalation combined with high pressure tunes 1T-TaS2 into an Ising superconductor with a dome-shaped superconducting phase and enhanced in-plane critical field.
motivation: The high-pressure behavior of low-dimensional materials is largely unexplored, and a synergistic tuning strategy could reveal emergent electronic phases.
method: Cetyltrimethylammonium cations are intercalated into bulk 1T-TaS2 to weaken interlayer coupling, followed by high-pressure transport measurements up to 58.1 GPa.
result: Superconductivity emerges with complete suppression of nearly commensurate charge density wave order, displays a dome-shaped evolution, and shows Ising signatures with in-plane upper critical field exceeding twice the Pauli limit.
conclusion: Intercalation plus pressure offers a powerful route to tune collective electronic states and search for emergent phenomena in low-dimensional materials.

title: Altermagnetism And Superconductivity: A Short Historical Review
authors: Hui Hu And Xia-Ji Liu Zhao Liu
abstract: This review is organized into three parts. In the first part, we explore the deep interconnections among three seemingly unrelated concepts in condensed matter physics: electronic liquid crystal (ELC) phases, multipole expansions, and altermagnetism (AM). At the heart of these phenomena lies a shared foundation: spin-momentum locking in the nonrelativistic regime. Originally proposed in the context of ELC phases, nonrelativistic spin-momentum locking (NRSML) was later elegantly incorporated into the formalism of multipole expansions. This framework can be further extended across multiple atomic sites, making it particularly effective for describing AMs, which host localized magnetic moments with anisotropic magnetization densities distributed over sublattices. In the second part, we examine superconducting (SC) phenomena associated with AM from three complementary perspectives. First, we investigate SC associated with NRSML Fermi surfaces (FSs), the unifying theme of the first part, highlighting a rich variety of unconventional SC states. These include finite-momentum pairing, -wave and spin-triplet SC, and topological Bogoliubov FSs, among others. We then review SC emerging from either static AM order or AM fluctuations. Finally, we discuss the possible competition and intertwining between AM order and SC, illustrated using the repulsive Hubbard model. Additional related topics are addressed in the concluding part. Overall, this work offers both an accessible introduction to the newly identified magnetic order known as AM and a conceptual guide for researchers aiming to harness the ensuing unconventional SC in the development of future quantum technologies.
tldr: A historical review connecting altermagnetism, superconductivity, and spin-momentum locking in condensed matter physics.
motivation: To provide an accessible introduction to altermagnetism and a conceptual guide for harnessing unconventional superconductivity in future quantum technologies.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical developments across electronic liquid crystal phases, multipole expansions, and altermagnetic order, with a focus on superconducting states in these systems.
result: It identifies a variety of unconventional superconducting states associated with nonrelativistic spin-momentum locking Fermi surfaces, static altermagnetic order, and altermagnetic fluctuations.
conclusion: Altermagnetism offers a rich platform for unconventional superconductivity, with potential implications for future quantum technologies.

title: Channel Formation Enhances Target Consumption By Chemotactic Active Brownian Particles
authors: Shahar Shinehorn And Yael Roichman Vladimir Yu Rudyak
abstract: In many situations, simply finding a target during a search is not enough. It is equally important to be able to return to that target repeatedly or to enable a larger community to locate and utilize it. While first passage time is commonly used to measure search success, relatively little is known about measures of repeated target encounters, such as the mean first passage count, and their rate over time. Here we compare an active Brownian particle model with central resetting, with and without chemotaxis. Searchers with no individual memory but shared environmental memory encode information about the target’s location in the environment, outperforming purely memoryless strategies by boosting the overall hit rate. We further show that this approach leads to a sublinear dependence of encounter rate on target size, reducing the impact of target size on a successful search and increasing the total utilization time of the target.
tldr: Active Brownian particles with chemotaxis and shared environmental memory achieve higher repeated target encounter rates and sublinear scaling with target size compared to memoryless searchers.
motivation: Finding a target once is often insufficient; repeated encounters and sustained utilization are important, yet measures such as mean first passage count and encounter rate are less understood.
method: The authors model an active Brownian particle with central resetting, comparing searchers with and without chemotaxis, and incorporate shared environmental memory through channel formation.
result: Shared environmental memory boosts the overall hit rate and leads to a sublinear dependence of encounter rate on target size, increasing total target utilization time.
conclusion: Environmental memory enhances target consumption by chemotactic active Brownian particles and reduces the impact of target size on search success.

title: Attosecond Molecular Physics In Large (bio) Molecules: A Perspective On An Unexplored Landscape
authors: V Despré, S Palakkal, E Munaro-Langloÿs And F Lépine
abstract: The 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized attosecond science and technology, which allows us to understand and control the properties of matter by accessing electron dynamics at the Angstrom length scale. Attosecond science and technology are currently being applied to investigate all phases of matter and have garnered particular attention in the field of light-induced processes in molecules. After two decades of development, an attosecond perspective on molecular processes has become a tangible reality thanks to advanced experiments and theories. However, so far, this has only been applied to small model systems. This article discusses the current state of the field and explores how it could expand to include the study of complex structures, including large biomolecules.
tldr: A perspective article surveying the state of attosecond molecular physics and outlining how it could be extended from small model systems to large complex biomolecules.
motivation: Attosecond science, recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize, has enabled access to electron dynamics on Angstrom length and sub-femtosecond time scales, but its application has so far been limited to small model molecules rather than complex biological systems.
method: Conceptual perspective and review of current experimental and theoretical capabilities in attosecond spectroscopy, together with a discussion of the challenges (e.g., decoherence, complexity, size) involved in extending these techniques to large (bio) molecules.
result: Identifies the methodological and physical obstacles that currently prevent attosecond techniques from being applied to large biomolecules, and proposes directions in which theory and experiment could be developed to reach this unexplored landscape.
conclusion: Attosecond molecular physics on large biomolecules is presented as an open frontier, requiring new experimental and theoretical advances before becoming a practical reality.

tldr: A collective decision-making model examining how different messaging strategies among communicating agents lead to the emergence of echo chambers.

conclusion: Messaging strategy is a key determinant of whether collective decision-making remains diverse and accurate or collapses into echo chambers, with implications for social, economic, and biological collective behavior.

abstract: Nanostructured targets have long been explored for controlling laser absorption and particle acceleration, but whether they survive the pre-pulse of a petawatt-class laser at realistic temporal contrast remains an open question. title: Singularities And The Divergence Of Spherical Harmonic Expansions: Axially Symmetric Planets

abstract: The region of convergence of the spherical harmonic expansion (SHE) is determined by the (generally complex) singularities of the gravitational potential. This complex analysis perspective is at the heart of recent rigorous results concerning the divergence properties of the SHE. In this paper we build physical intuition for these general mathematical results using illustrative examples (some familiar and some new) of idealized planets for which the analysis is particularly explicit. This approach provides new methods to determine the region of convergence, without computing and analyzing expansion coefficients, and gives a novel geometric understanding of the divergence phenomenon. It also explains the fundamental origin of the numerical instabilities inherent to polyhedral models of planets. For the sake of clarity, we illustrate this new approach for the special case of axisymmetric planets of constant density, with explicit comparisons, but the key ideas do not rely on these restrictions.
tldr: The paper studies convergence of spherical harmonic expansions for gravitational potentials of idealized planets using complex singularity analysis.
motivation: Recent rigorous mathematical results on SHE divergence need physical intuition and explicit examples to better understand convergence regions and numerical instabilities.
method: The authors use complex analysis of potential singularities and illustrate with axially symmetric constant-density planet models, comparing explicit cases.
result: They provide new geometric methods to determine the region of convergence without computing expansion coefficients and explain the origin of numerical instabilities in polyhedral planet models.
conclusion: The singularity-based perspective clarifies SHE divergence and offers practical insight for planetary gravity modeling, though it is outside quantum information and related research directions.

title: Turbulent Magnetogenesis And Large-scale Magnetic Dynamo Amplification In Ion–electron Plasmas
authors: Fabio Bacchini, Francesco Pucci, Sergio Servidio, Francesco Valentini And William H Matthaeus
abstract: Using fully kinetic simulations that capture unprecedentedly large (from electron to ion) scales, we study magnetogenesis driven by continuous large-scale forcing until nonlinear dynamo saturation. We uncover a two-stage mechanism in collisionless ion–electron plasmas whose dynamics diverge dramatically from the pair-plasma case. In the first phase, electron pressure anisotropy triggers electron-Weibel modes, seeding small-scale magnetic fields. Then, a second growth phase emerges when the more massive ions develop their own strong anisotropy and drive ion-Weibel-type modes; concurrently, a Biermann-battery mechanism contributes to amplifying the magnetic field. This combined dynamics provides a tenfold amplification of the magnetic field in comparison to the pair-plasma case. Over long times, dynamo action continues until the system reaches a statistical steady state. This self-consistent kinetic mechanism provides a plausible explanation for robust magnetogenesis wherever an external forcing continuously stirs the plasma.
tldr: Fully kinetic simulations reveal a two-stage magnetogenesis mechanism in collisionless ion-electron plasmas, driven by electron and ion Weibel instabilities and a Biermann battery, leading to strong magnetic field amplification.
motivation: The origin and amplification of magnetic fields in astrophysical plasmas remain important open problems, especially where collisions are negligible and dynamics span electron-to-ion scales.
method: The authors use fully kinetic simulations with continuous large-scale forcing, capturing unprecedentedly large ranges of spatial and temporal scales until nonlinear dynamo saturation.
result: They find a two-stage growth: first electron pressure anisotropy triggers electron-Weibel modes, then ion anisotropy drives ion-Weibel modes while a Biermann battery contributes, yielding a tenfold magnetic field amplification over the pair-plasma case.
conclusion: This self-consistent kinetic mechanism provides a plausible explanation for robust magnetogenesis in continuously stirred collisionless plasmas and sustains dynamo action until statistical steady state.

title: Gibbs State Preparation For Commuting Hamiltonian: Mapping To Classical Gibbs Sampling
authors: Yeongwoo Hwang And Jiaqing Jiang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2209 (2026).

Gibbs state preparation, or Gibbs sampling, is a key computational technique extensively used in physics, statistics, and other scientific fields. Recent efforts for designing fast mixing Gibbs samplers for quantum Hamiltonians have largely focused on commuting local Hamiltonians (CLHs), a non-trivial subclass of Hamiltonians which include highly entangled systems such as the Toric code and quantum double model. Most previous Gibbs samplers relied on simulating the Davies generator, which is a Lindbladian associated with the thermalization process in nature. Instead of using the Davies generator, we design a different Gibbs sampler for various CLHs by giving a reduction to classical Hamiltonians, in the sense that one can efficiently prepare the Gibbs state for some CLH [MATH] on a quantum computer as long as one can efficiently do classical Gibbs sampling for the corresponding classical Hamiltonian [MATH]. We demonstrate that our Gibbs sampler is able to replicate state-of-the-art results as well as prepare the Gibbs state in regimes which were previously unknown, such as the low temperature region, as long as there exists fast mixing Gibbs samplers for the corresponding classical Hamiltonians. Our reductions are as follows. – If [MATH] is a 2-local qudit CLH, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are no classical qubits, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian on a planar graph. As an example, our algorithm can prepare the Gibbs state for the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in [MATH] time. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are classical qubits, assuming that quantum terms are uniformly correctable, then [MATH] is a constant-local classical Hamiltonian.

title: Advances In Laser-assisted Nuclear Decay And Nuclear Excitation
authors: Q Xiao, J H Cheng, Y Y Xu, Y T Zou, Z Z Ren, A Ya Dzyublik And T P Yu
abstract: From the synthesis and evolution of the elements to the celestial nuclear processes of stellar explosions and neutron star mergers, nuclear physics is the foundation of our understanding of the Universe. After more than a century of progress, the field of nuclear physics remains vibrant. The rapid advancement of laser technology has opened unprecedented avenues in nuclear physics, driven by the interdisciplinary convergence of laser physics, nuclear structure, plasma science, and quantum dynamics. This emerging field enables studies on laser-induced nuclear excitation, laser-assisted nuclear decay, and precision manipulation of nuclear isomers for optical clocks. This review comprehensively examines the research achievements over the past decade regarding the influence of lasers on radioactive charged-particle emissions and nuclear excitation. Regarding theoretical developments, the review details various methods used to evaluate the interactions between lasers and nuclei, including the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for decay, proton radioactivity, and two-proton radioactivity and Fermi’s golden rule for nuclear excitation as well as the application and advancement of various theoretical models and approximation methods. In experimental research, the review synthesizes significant breakthroughs in laser-induced nuclear excitation experiments, particularly emphasizing the excitation of the Th, Kr, and Sc. These achievements provide essential groundwork for future breakthroughs in both fundamental nuclear science and its broader technological applications.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances in laser-assisted nuclear decay and nuclear excitation over the past decade.
motivation: Laser technology advancements enable new studies in nuclear physics, bridging laser physics, nuclear structure, plasma science, and quantum dynamics.
method: Reviews theoretical frameworks (time-dependent Schrödinger equation, Fermi's golden rule) and experimental breakthroughs in laser-induced nuclear excitation of Th, Kr, and Sc.
result: Summarizes significant progress in understanding laser-nucleus interactions and manipulating nuclear isomers for optical clocks.
conclusion: Provides essential groundwork for future fundamental nuclear science and technological applications.
